actions.result: Able to stand single-leg briefly with mild wobble; reports apprehension and sensation of instability with partial squat/pivot motion, no immediate giving-way during test

actions.name: Review knee x-ray report (obtained day of injury)
actions.result: 3-view right knee x-ray: no fracture, no dislocation, growth plates closed, joint spaces preserved, small suprapatellar joint effusion

actions.name: Review emergency department/urgent care note from day of injury

actions.name: Review physical therapy prehab referral status
actions.result: No physical therapy visits attended yet; referral placed by primary care at time of injury but not yet scheduled

actions.name: Review growth plate status for surgical planning
actions.result: Distal femoral and proximal tibial physes are closed/fused on imaging, consistent with skeletal maturity; standard adult-type ACL reconstruction techniques are appropriate

actions.name: Review inflammatory/infection labs if effusion were concerning (CBC, CRP)
actions.result: CBC and CRP not clinically indicated given classic traumatic mechanism and non-infectious exam; not drawn

actions.name: Assess functional stability and readiness for pivoting sports in current state
actions.result: Current subjective instability with pivoting activities and two episodes of giving-way on stairs; not safe for return to cutting/pivoting sport without surgical stabilization and structured rehabilitation

artifacts.title: MRI Right Knee Without Contrast
artifacts.author: Radiology — Dr. A. Nguyen
artifacts.body: FINDINGS: Complete full-thickness tear of the anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) mid-substance with wavy contour and absent fibers on sagittal sequences. Small peripheral tear of the posterior horn/body junction of the lateral meniscus, non-displaced, stable appearing. Bone marrow edema (bone bruise) involving the lateral femoral condyle and posterolateral tibial plateau, consistent with pivot-shift mechanism. Medial meniscus intact. PCL, MCL, and LCL intact. Articular cartilage preserved throughout, no focal chondral defect. Distal femoral and proximal tibial growth plates are closed/fused. Small joint effusion. IMPRESSION: 1. Complete ACL tear. 2. Small non-displaced lateral meniscus tear. 3. Bone contusions typical of pivot injury. 4. Skeletally mature growth plates.

artifacts.title: Right Knee X-ray, 3 views (day of injury)
artifacts.author: Radiology — Dr. T. Olsen
artifacts.body: FINDINGS: No acute fracture or dislocation. Joint spaces preserved. Small suprapatellar effusion. Growth plates closed. IMPRESSION: No fracture. Effusion noted, correlate clinically.

artifacts.title: Urgent Care Note — Date of Injury
artifacts.author: Dr. R. Castillo, Urgent Care
artifacts.body: 17-year-old female presents with acute right knee injury during soccer match approximately 2 hours prior. Reports planting right foot and pivoting when she felt a pop and immediate pain, followed by rapid swelling. Unable to bear full weight initially. On exam: moderate effusion, limited ROM due to pain and swelling, ligamentous exam deferred due to guarding and effusion, distal pulses intact, sensation intact. Placed in hinged knee brace locked in extension for comfort, given crutches for partial weight-bearing, ice/elevation instructed, ibuprofen for pain. X-ray obtained, no fracture. Referred to orthopedic surgery for MRI and further evaluation. Physical therapy prehabilitation referral placed.

facts.chart: 17-year-old female presents for review of MRI results and discussion of treatment options after right knee injury 3 weeks ago.
facts.says: I'm here to find out what my MRI showed and what we're going to do about my knee — I've got a big tournament coming up.

facts.chart: Injury occurred during soccer match when patient planted right foot and pivoted; felt a pop.
facts.says: I was cutting to the left during a game and my foot kind of stuck in the turf — I felt a pop in my knee right away.

facts.chart: Knee swelled within approximately 2 hours of injury.
facts.says: It blew up like a balloon within like an hour or two, it was huge by the time my mom got me home.

facts.chart: Knee has given way twice on stairs since the injury.
facts.says: It's buckled on me twice going down the stairs at home, it's scary, like my knee just isn't there for a second.

facts.chart: Initially unable to bear full weight; now ambulates without crutches but avoids pivoting.
facts.says: I couldn't put weight on it the first day, but now I can walk fine, I just don't trust it when I turn.

facts.chart: Pain currently mild, rated 2/10 at rest, worse with twisting activity.
facts.says: It barely hurts just sitting around, maybe a 2 out of 10, but if I try to twist it, it's way worse.

facts.chart: Denies true locking or catching sensation.
facts.says: It hasn't ever gotten stuck or locked up on me, just feels wobbly sometimes.

facts.chart: Residual mild swelling present most days, worse after activity.
facts.says: It's still a little puffy most days, especially after I've been up and around a lot.

facts.chart: Has been using hinged knee brace intermittently, not consistently as directed.
facts.says: I wear the brace sometimes, honestly, it's bulky under my jeans so I skip it some days.

facts.chart: Patient has a college recruiting showcase tournament in approximately 10 weeks and wants to know if she can play in a brace.
facts.says: There's a huge college showcase in like ten weeks and I need to know if I can just play in a brace.

facts.chart: Patient expresses fear that missing the showcase will end her chances of being recruited.
facts.says: If I miss this tournament, I feel like coaches are just going to forget I exist.

facts.chart: Patient reports frustration and anxiety about timeline and loss of control.
facts.says: I've worked my whole life for this and now it feels like it's all slipping away because of one stupid turn.

facts.chart: Mother present in adjacent room, involved in care decisions and will participate if invited.
facts.says: My mom's right in the next room, she wants to be part of this conversation too.

facts.chart: Taking combined oral contraceptive for menstrual cycle regulation, unrelated to current injury.
facts.says: I'm on the pill, just for my periods, nothing to do with my knee.

facts.chart: No prior knee injuries, surgeries, or instability episodes before this injury.
facts.says: This is the first time anything's ever happened to this knee, never had problems before.

facts.chart: Mother reports her own ACL tear and reconstruction in her 20s, recovered well and returned to recreational sports.
facts.says: Funny enough, my mom tore the same ligament years ago and she's totally fine now, so that gives me some hope.

facts.chart: Denies numbness, tingling, or color change in the foot/leg.
facts.says: No numbness or weird color in my foot or toes, that's all normal.

facts.chart: Denies pain or swelling in other joints.
facts.says: No other joints are bothering me, just the one knee.

facts.chart: Taking ibuprofen 400 mg as needed, roughly 2-3 times per week currently.
facts.says: I take the ibuprofen when it's really bothering me, maybe a couple times a week now.

facts.chart: Has not yet attended any physical therapy sessions despite referral placed three weeks ago.
facts.says: I haven't actually made it to physical therapy yet, it's been hard to get an appointment with school and everything.

facts.chart: Attending school full days, uses elevator when possible, avoids stairs when able.
facts.says: I'm at school full days, I try to take the elevator now instead of stairs when I can.

facts.chart: Driving without difficulty, no limitations noted.
facts.says: I'm driving fine, that part hasn't been a problem.

facts.chart: Lives with mother and younger sibling; father lives in another state.
facts.says: It's just me, my mom, and my little brother at home most of the time.

facts.chart: Plays club soccer year-round and on varsity high school team; central midfielder, team captain.
facts.says: I play club soccer basically all year plus varsity for my high school, I'm the captain this year.

facts.chart: Patient has heard from teammates that some athletes play on torn ACLs with a brace and wants to know if that applies to her.
facts.says: One of my teammates said she played a whole season on a torn ACL with just a brace, is that something I could do?

facts.chart: Expresses some fear about surgery itself, in addition to timeline concerns.
facts.says: I'm not gonna lie, the surgery part scares me too, not just missing the tournament.

facts.chart: Reports eating a generally balanced diet, no recent weight change.
facts.says: I eat pretty normal, nothing's really changed with my weight or appetite.

facts.chart: Swelling increases notably after attempting any jogging or pivoting movements, which she has tried twice against instructions.
facts.says: I tried jogging a little in the backyard twice just to test it, and it swelled up both times afterward.

facts.chart: Does not recall whether brace is set to allow full range of motion versus restricted range; has not followed up on this detail.
facts.says: Honestly I don't really know if the brace is set to let my knee bend all the way or not, I never asked.

facts.chart: Patient initially believes recovery might take only 6-8 weeks based on online research.
facts.says: I read online some people are back in like six to eight weeks, is that realistic for me?

facts.chart: Mother has concerns about insurance coverage and cost of surgery versus physical therapy alone, has not yet contacted insurer.
facts.says: My mom mentioned she's worried about what insurance will cover, surgery versus just doing therapy.

facts.chart: No prior surgeries of any kind.
facts.says: I've never had any surgery before, this would be my first.

mismatches.patientClaim: Patient reports wearing the hinged knee brace at least intermittently since the injury and attempting to follow activity precautions.
mismatches.recordEvidence: Physical therapy referral note documents no prehab visits attended and ongoing high-risk activity (patient tried jogging/pivoting twice despite instructions), with brace use inconsistent per patient's own admission — overall adherence to the structured protection plan is incomplete.
mismatches.teachingPoint: Even well-intentioned, motivated patients may underestimate gaps in adherence to bracing and activity restriction; explicitly reconcile stated behavior with functional reports (giving-way episodes, self-initiated jogging) before counseling on risk of further injury.

mismatches.patientClaim: Patient believes a 6-8 week return to sport is realistic based on online information.
mismatches.recordEvidence: Range of motion trend chart shows slow, incomplete recovery of motion even at 3 weeks (125 degrees active flexion, not yet symmetric with contralateral 140 degrees), illustrating that early motion alone is not synonymous with readiness for cutting/pivoting sport, which standard ACL reconstruction protocols require passing criteria-based testing with a minimum of about 9 months and often longer.
mismatches.teachingPoint: Online anecdotes about rapid return to sport often reflect selection bias or non-pivoting sports; evidence-based ACL reconstruction rehabilitation is criteria-based (minimum ~9 months, graft maturation and neuromuscular readiness testing), not determined by symptom resolution or motion milestones alone.

objectives.text: Elicit a mechanism-of-injury history consistent with a non-contact pivoting ACL injury, including the pop, rapid effusion, and subsequent instability episodes.

Perform and interpret a guided remote knee examination (inspection, active ROM, subjective instability/apprehension questioning) recognizing its limitations compared to in-person exam, including the impossibility of a valid remote Lachman/anterior drawer test.

Accurately interpret and explain the MRI findings (complete ACL tear, small stable lateral meniscus tear, bone bruising, closed growth plates) in lay terms appropriate for a teenage patient and parent.

Counsel on operative versus non-operative management for a skeletally mature competitive pivoting athlete, correctly discouraging play on a torn ACL in a brace given risk of further meniscal/chondral injury and recurrent instability.

Set a realistic, evidence-based return-to-sport expectation (criteria-based testing, minimum ~9 months, potentially well beyond 12 months) and address the patient's goal conflict with the 10-week showcase tournament with empathy.

Identify the gap in prehabilitation engagement and reconcile the patient's self-reported adherence with the referral record, then provide a prehab plan and appropriate referral/handback to physical therapy.

profile.summary: A 17-year-old competitive soccer player with a complete ACL tear, small stable lateral meniscus tear, and bone bruising on MRI after a classic pivoting injury presents for results review and treatment planning. The case tests the resident's ability to perform a guided remote knee exam, explain imaging findings in lay terms, counsel on operative versus non-operative management for a skeletally mature pivoting athlete (explicitly addressing why bracing alone is unsafe for return to cutting sports), and navigate a realistic 9-12 month return-to-sport timeline against the patient's urgent desire to play in a 10-week showcase tournament.
profile.title: Complete ACL Tear in a Skeletally Mature Teen Athlete — Results Review and Return-to-Sport Planning

answerKey.primaryProblem: Complete right ACL tear with small stable lateral meniscus tear and bone bruising in a skeletally mature 17-year-old competitive pivoting athlete, three weeks post-injury with ongoing episodic instability.
differential: Isolated complete ACL tear (confirmed on MRI)
Combined ACL and meniscal injury (confirmed: small stable lateral meniscus tear)
Multiligamentous knee injury (excluded: MCL/LCL/PCL intact on MRI)
Patellar instability/dislocation (excluded: mechanism and exam not consistent, no patellar apprehension described)
Tibial plateau or physeal fracture (excluded: x-ray negative, growth plates closed)
keyFindings: Classic non-contact pivot mechanism with audible/felt pop and rapid (within 2 hours) effusion
Two episodes of knee giving-way on stairs since injury, plus swelling recurrence after self-initiated jogging/pivoting attempts
MRI: complete mid-substance ACL tear, small non-displaced stable lateral meniscus tear, bone bruising of lateral femoral condyle and posterolateral tibial plateau, closed growth plates
Guided remote exam notable for residual effusion, mild quadriceps atrophy, incomplete terminal flexion, and subjective instability on self-performed stability testing and pivoting/squat maneuvers
Inconsistent brace adherence and no physical therapy prehab visits attended despite three-week-old referral
plan: Explain MRI findings in plain language to patient and mother, emphasizing complete ACL tear with closed growth plates allowing standard adult-type reconstruction technique if surgery chosen

Counsel against return to pivoting/cutting sport (including the 10-week showcase) in a brace alone given confirmed complete ACL tear, ongoing instability episodes, and risk of further meniscal/chondral injury

Discuss operative (ACL reconstruction, timing options including graft choice discussion deferred to full surgical consult) versus non-operative management (activity modification, bracing, physical therapy) and shared decision-making given patient's competitive pivoting sport goals

Set realistic return-to-sport expectations: criteria-based clearance with a minimum of approximately 9 months post-reconstruction, based on graft maturation and validated functional/neuromuscular/strength testing rather than a fixed calendar date, and explain that timing can extend well beyond 12 months if objective criteria are not yet met
Address the gap in prehabilitation: escalate/expedite physical therapy referral for prehab (quadriceps strengthening, effusion control, ROM) prior to any surgical date
Advise strict avoidance of further unsupervised pivoting/jogging trials pending stabilization plan to reduce risk of secondary meniscal or chondral injury
Arrange follow-up visit for shared decision on surgical timing and formal surgical consent discussion if family elects reconstruction; involve mother in decision-making given patient's age
redFlags: Recurrent giving-way episodes increasing risk of secondary meniscal/chondral damage if pivoting activity continues unprotected
Patient's own activity (unsupervised jogging trials) outside of recommended restrictions while awaiting treatment decision
Delay in prehabilitation engagement that could affect surgical readiness and timeline
educationPoints: A complete ACL tear with closed growth plates in a skeletally mature teenager is treated using standard adult ACL reconstruction principles, not pediatric growth-plate-sparing techniques
Playing competitive pivoting sport on a torn ACL, even with a brace, does not restore rotational stability and carries meaningful risk of further meniscal or cartilage injury

Return-to-sport after ACL reconstruction should be criteria-based rather than purely time-based: current evidence supports a minimum of approximately 9 months, driven by graft biological maturation and passing validated functional/strength/neuromuscular testing, with return often extending well past 12 months if criteria are not met
Prehabilitation (quadriceps strengthening, effusion control, achieving full motion) before surgery improves post-operative outcomes and should begin promptly
Shared decision-making should explicitly involve both the patient and parent given the patient's age, balancing athletic goals with safety
